why: The statute adds an identification condition to casting a counted ballot.
The condition can require documents or use of a lawful alternative/cure by an eligible voter.
Observed aggregate turnout can remain near its previous rate when affected voters satisfy the condition or receive mobilization help.
The study estimated a small overall effect; it did not erase each voter’s legal requirement.
The bedrock is a voter’s documentation, actual statutory cure and decision to vote.
conditions: Study coverage ends2018; later statutory changes and injunctions require current authority research.
ID acceptance, free-ID access, cure rules and outreach differ by state.
Published uncertainty includes turnout decreases and increases.
changes.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal removes the extra statutory condition; past uncounted votes do not return. A repeal effect is not automatically the negative of an adoption estimate.
changes.who: Eligible voters subject to the actual identification rule; nonwhite relative turnout is a separate reported estimate, not an every-group identical effect.
changes.lagWhy: The legal rule acts at an election/cure deadline; the estimate pools elections within the study window, not a measured zero-month delivery lag.

why: A polling-place identification rule does not itself register or unregister a resident.
Registration changes only through a separate eligible application, cancellation or agency registration action.
Voters may respond to requirements, but the study measured a small aggregate registration estimate.
The uncertainty interval permits either direction.
The bedrock is the resident’s eligibility and an actual legally recognized registration transaction.
conditions: Registration verification requirements are distinct from polling-place ID.
An enacted bill that changes both mechanisms must expose both provisions.

changes.reverseOnRepeal: Repealing polling-place ID does not manufacture registration transactions or restore separately cancelled registration.
changes.who: People eligible to register under their jurisdiction’s actual registration law.
changes.lagWhy: A registration effect requires a registration transaction and legal deadline; no measured instantaneous registration writer is established.

studies.finding: Published abstract says termlimits decrease voterturnout.

studies.coverage: comparative state aggregate and district-level legislative elections

changes.anchor: California and comparative-state studies report different signed findings. No researched universal near-zero effect or numeric range is established.
why: A binding limit prevents an otherwise eligible incumbent from seeking another term.
An open seat changes the candidates voters can select.
Competition and attachment to the departing incumbent can pull participation in different directions.
The measured turnout response depends on the electorate and election.
The bedrock is an actual legal candidacy bar and voters’ decisions from the changed candidate set.
conditions: California’s1976–2004 estimate is not a nationwide zero effect.
Comparativestate evidence reports an increase; effect sizes and uncertainty still require the fulltables.
Lifetime, consecutive and service-break rules alter which seats actually open.
changes.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal changes future eligibility; it does not reinstate priorholders or reverse pastturnout.
changes.who: Incumbents legally barred and voters in their affected legislative districts.
changes.lagWhy: The rule matters at the next applicable candidacy/election; no pooled nationwide zero-month causal response is established.
